doc.title: Wendell Harrison interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 17, 2022 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Jazz in America today versus the 1960s and 70s
summary: Asked where jazz fits now, Harrison describes his eclectic base in bebop and Ellington, work with Carl Craig and Proof, and contrasts live-audience gigs then with academic playing now.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Well it’s been a labor of love and a labor of soul and everything else in between and I admire that, your passion for it. So I’d like to wrap up today with a question about jazz in

society. Now you’re describing this intense relationship with local musicians and spreading it worldwide and when I think back to the swing era that jazz and swing had this social dancing aspect and entertainment value. Do you have a thought about jazz in America now? Where does it fit? Does it have a distinctive character in America now?

Yeah, a lot of different jazz styles now as you know. You know I’m 80 years old. My concept comes out of — the genesis of my concept came from the 50s from the bebop era. And when I write, I’m writing — like Oliver Lake —not Oliver Lake but Oliver Nelson — Oliver, Duke Ellington and my head is like that. My head is grounded in that sound although I write all kinds of ways. I’ve got skills to write all kinds of ways you know. But you know I even learned how to deal with hip hop, I mean techno you know. Because I worked with Carl Craig. Then I started to deal with rap, like I worked with a guy by the name of Proof put out a record called “Grown Folks Shit.” That’s the rappers. So I’m kind of in terms of me, I’m kind of eclectic with a jazz base, a jazz foundation but I’m eclectic. I deal with African concepts, I deal with Latin concepts, hip hop, but really coming from a jazz perspective. I use all these elements. I even use Sun Ra, but sparingly. I’ll go out, but I always come back to my base, my jazz concept. I might go out and play some space music for a couple of minutes but I always come back to who I am. And that’s how it’s been selling over the years. Jazz today it’s just about the college campuses. University campuses today, which is more academic, more academic. Because they don’t have the engagements that we had back in the 60s and 70s. We was playing this music every week for a live audience. A live audience every week, we were playing gigs, gigs. So we were playing for the audience and trying to get approval from the audience and at the same time we were trying to sell records too. Because if we went too far out our records wouldn’t sell. So we would learn how to play and improvise, including melody and harmonics that everybody could actually digest, the average person could digest. The students now, it seems to me, they’re playing for themselves academically and they find out how many notes can you play at once. You know you can play all these notes, how fast can you play? And they have great technique but the story often is not really as prolific as the stories that we told back in the 50s and 60s, this coming from my point of view.
